stops.name: Buenos Aires, birth into the Ocampo-Aguirre house
stops.campa: Ramona Victoria Epifanía Rufina Ocampo is born into one of the old fortunes of Buenos Aires, the eldest of six daughters of the engineer Manuel Ocampo and Ramona Aguirre, a family whose name on both sides runs back to the colonial founding of the River Plate. The house is large, French-shuttered, staffed; the girls will grow up between Buenos Aires and the family's summer ground at San Isidro, catechized in French before Spanish. Victoria will say of her first schoolbook only that it was French; the whole of her childhood is contained in that single, exact complaint.
stops.quote: The alphabet-book from which I learned to read was French.

stops.name: San Isidro, summers at the villa her father is building
stops.campa: North of the city, on the bluff above the brown river, Manuel Ocampo has begun to raise a three-story summer house of Renaissance and Victorian airs on the Calle Elortondo in Beccar, begun in 1891, the year after Victoria's birth. The child summers here among unfinished galleries and gardens still being planted, the river wide and slow below the barranca. She does not yet know that this house, later called Villa Ocampo, will become the stage of her whole life: the port at which Tagore lands ill, where Stravinsky rehearses, where a magazine that does not exist yet will be dreamed.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the governess and the forbidden stage
stops.campa: Educated entirely at home by French governesses, never sent to school, Victoria discovers in these years a passion that will be denied her: the theater. She takes lessons in declamation with joy and with the foreknowledge, even as a girl, that the joy is aborted in advance. Her father has told his daughters plainly that if any one of them becomes an actress he will shoot himself the same day. She writes to her friend Delfina Bunge that she was born to act, that she carries theater in her blood; she will never dare to contradict her parents, and the vocation goes underground, to surface thirty years later on an opera stage for a single night.
stops.quote: I was born to act. I carry theater in my blood. I am a great artist, and without theater I have neither joy nor peace. It is my vocation.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Delfina Bunge, quoted in 'Victoria Ocampo y el teatro: ¿un amor fugaz?'

stops.name: Paris, first crossing to the Europe of the mind
stops.campa: The family crosses to Europe as it does every few years, but this time the sixteen-year-old is permitted, half-clandestinely, to audit lectures at the Sorbonne and the Collège de France. She sits among students who do not know her, listening above all to Henri Bergson, whose account of duration and memory will mark her thinking for the rest of her life. She writes her first prose in French, as she has since 1901; French is the language of her interior, Spanish still a language she must earn, and will not fully claim as a writer's instrument until a Spaniard teaches her to hear it.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, reading the Comedy as a private confession
stops.campa: In these same years the young woman falls into the Divine Comedy the way one falls into an illness or a love: not as a schoolbook but as a mirror. She does not read Dante, she says later, she lives him; Francesca da Rimini's damnation for love and Beatrice's radiant remove become, for a girl already dreaming of a love and a vocation both forbidden her, the poles of her own unwritten life. Fifteen years on this reading will become her first book, De Francesca a Beatrice, written first in French, the confession of what the Comedy meant to her at this exact threshold.
stops.quote: Yo no leía a Dante, lo vivía. (I did not read Dante, I lived him.)
stops.quote_source: De Francesca a Beatrice a través de la Divina Comedia (1924), retrospective testimony

stops.name: Buenos Aires, marriage to Bernardo de Estrada
stops.campa: At twenty-two, under the enormous pressure of a class that does not let its daughters remain unmarried and does not permit divorce, Victoria marries Luis Bernardo de Estrada, called Monaco. The marriage is a catastrophe from the first year: within months husband and wife are living separate lives under a single roof neither wants, bound by a Church and a code that will not undo the sacrament. She will spend the following decade privately, in her own account, imprisoned in a house she cannot legally leave, until a passion she does not choose and cannot resist breaks the arrangement from within.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the encounter with Ortega y Gasset
stops.campa: In a private house in Buenos Aires, Victoria is introduced to José Ortega y Gasset, in the country on his first American tour. The meeting has, she will write decades later, the dimension of a revelation: through this one Spaniard she discovers Spain itself, a Spain she had not suspected under the schoolroom's dead Castilian. It is the beginning of an epistolary friendship that will run for thirty years and more than a hundred letters, and it is Ortega, together with Waldo Frank, who will eventually push her toward the one act that outlasts every one of her love affairs: founding a magazine.
stops.quote: En él descubrí España. Una España deslumbrante. (In him, I discovered Spain. A dazzling Spain.)
stops.quote_source: Written 1965, ten years after Ortega's death

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the passion for Julián Martínez
stops.campa: Julián Martínez, her husband's own cousin, a career diplomat, falls in love with the young wife trapped in his relative's failed marriage, and she with him; it is a passion that will last, by her own later confession, eighteen years, deeper than any love she will know before or after. She will not divorce Estrada, cannot under the law of her country and her Church, but she leaves the shared house; the affair with Martínez runs underground through the following two decades, feeding directly into the reading of Dante's Francesca that becomes her first book and into the woman who founds Sur.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the apartment on Garay street
stops.campa: Victoria formally separates from Estrada and takes rooms of her own on Calle Garay near Parque Lezama, an ordinary act by later measure and a small scandal by the measure of Buenos Aires society in 1920: a married woman of her class living alone. The gesture matters more than the address; it is the first time she answers to no household but her own, reads and writes at hours she sets, receives whom she chooses. Everything that follows, the magazine, the house opened to poets and dissidents, begins in this small act of a room taken in her own name.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, reading of Gandhi through Romain Rolland
stops.campa: Romain Rolland's biography of Mahatma Gandhi, published in French the year before, reaches Victoria in the same season she is host to Tagore; the two Indias, the poet's and the Mahatma's, arrive in her life almost as a single continent. She reads Gandhi with the same devotion she brings to Dante, and the admiration becomes durable: through the following decades, across Tagore's circle and later Nehru's and Indira Gandhi's, India remains for her not an exoticism but a second intellectual homeland, a source of the non-violence and the spiritual seriousness she measures European politics against as fascism gathers.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the news that Tagore will pass through
stops.campa: It is announced that Rabindranath Tagore, the Bengali poet crowned with the Nobel Prize a decade before, will pass through Buenos Aires on his way to Peru. Those who already know his verse, through his own English versions or Gide's French ones, begin to wait for him as for a planet's transit; Victoria will write that his arrival was the great event of the year for the city and one of the great events of her own life. She has no notion yet that fever and a ship's doctor will deliver the poet directly into her hands.
stops.quote: Su llegada sería el gran acontecimiento del año. Para mí, fue uno de los grandes acontecimientos de mi vida.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the port, an ailing poet disembarks
stops.campa: The ship carrying Tagore toward Lima puts in at Buenos Aires; he has fallen seriously ill with influenza in mid-ocean and his doctors will not let him continue. He disembarks a stranger in a country he had not meant to visit, sixty-three years old, plainly frail. Victoria Ocampo, thirty-four, an admirer who has read him for a decade, arranges within days for his convalescence to be private, comfortable, and near her: a small house called Villa Miralrío in San Isidro, on the same bluff above the river where her own family's villa stands, is found and readied for him.
